scenes.visual: Big navy hook text pops word by word; Norb peeks curious from below.
scenes.cardText: Why do some of the most testosterone-fueled people become the most generous leaders?
scenes.voiceover: Why do some of the most testosterone-fueled people you know become the most generous, disciplined leaders?

scenes.visual: One navy 'T' amplifier; coral AGGRESS=WIN and teal COOPERATE=WIN pills alternate; the behavior below flips fist ↔ handshake.
scenes.voiceover: Testosterone does not cause aggression. It amplifies your sensitivity to status. What you do about that depends on what wins respect around you.

scenes.visual: Rank ladder: bottom-rank creature trembles, top-rank wears a crown. Status drive made literal.
scenes.voiceover: So calling it the aggression hormone is wrong. It is a status hormone — and in the wrong culture, the drive for rank takes the ugliest path available.

scenes.visual: The navy circle springs wider; a coral outsider enters and turns teal; a warm mustard pulse blooms.
scenes.voiceover: The move: deliberately pick environments where kindness and competence win. Your status drive is fuel — the direction it takes depends on where you point it.

scenes.visual: THE SCIENCE card; contextFlip amplifier below showing the same T driving opposite behaviors. Norb curious.
scenes.cardText: The challenge hypothesis: testosterone surges at status challenges, then amplifies whatever the social context rewards — aggression or generosity.
scenes.voiceover: The challenge hypothesis: testosterone surges in response to status challenges, then amplifies whatever that context rewards — aggression, or generosity.

scenes.visual: TRY THIS card; widenCircle visual below. Norb celebrating.
scenes.cardText:
Next time you feel competitive:
ask what wins respect here — then channel it there.
scenes.voiceover: Next time you feel the urge to compete, ask what actually wins respect here — then aim the drive there.
